The number of locations is the other factor. Each branch has its own tables, staff and guests, so ArtOfMenu prices each branch separately.

A QR menu has a fixed monthly cost and no reprints. It will not replace every paper copy, and some guests will still ask for one. It pays off most in places that change prices often, run daily specials or serve guests who read other languages.

design.title: QR Menu Design: Stylish, Clear and Yours | ArtOfMenu
design.description: How to get a stylish, beautiful QR menu: photos, readable text, your brand and your own domain. What ArtOfMenu's layout does, and what it does not.
design.h1: A stylish QR menu design starts with your photos.
design.lead: A beautiful QR menu comes from three things: good photos, readable text and a layout that stays out of the way. ArtOfMenu provides the clean layout, and your photos and words do the rest.
design.answer: Good QR menu design means guests can read the menu on a small screen, see what each dish looks like and recognize your business. ArtOfMenu uses one clean, consistent layout for every menu, filled with your product photos, item descriptions and allergen details, on your own domain. It has no ready-made themes or custom code uploads.

sections.h2: Why design affects what guests order
body: On a phone, guests skim. They look at photos first, then names, then prices. A clear layout makes it easy to compare two dishes. A cluttered one makes guests settle for the first familiar thing. Items that never get noticed never get ordered.
ArtOfMenu's menu reports show where this happens. They flag items guests see but rarely open, and items they open but never order. Both are design questions as much as kitchen questions.

sections.h2: Photos do most of the work
body: You do not need a professional shoot. A recent phone, a clean table near a window and a few minutes before service is enough for most dishes.
bullets: Shoot in daylight rather than under warm kitchen lights
Use the same angle and background within a section so the list looks calm
Show the real portion on the plate you actually serve it on
Leave an item without a photo rather than using a stock image

sections.h2: Text that reads well on a phone
body: Keep item names short and descriptions to one line. Say what is in the dish and how it is cooked. “Charred leeks, hazelnut, brown butter” tells a guest more than a paragraph about the chef's inspiration.
Put allergen information on the item itself, where guests expect to find it. Group sections the way people order: drinks, small plates, mains, desserts.

sections.h2: Your brand, on your own domain
body: When a guest scans, the menu opens on your business's own domain. The address bar shows your name, which matters to guests who hesitate before tapping an unfamiliar link. Beyond that, your brand lives in your photos, your item names and the way you write about your food.

To set expectations clearly: ArtOfMenu does not offer a theme gallery or a design service, and you cannot upload your own HTML or CSS. Every menu uses the same clean layout, built for reading on a phone. If you want a fully custom look, a bespoke website is the better route.

sections.h2: Design that adapts during the day
body: On the Smart plan, the order of the menu responds to the weather. When it gets cold, hot drinks move up, while cold drinks and items about to run out move down. The layout guests know stays the same, and the most fitting items rise to the top.

faq.q: Can I customize the design of my QR menu?
faq.a: You control the content that shapes the look: photos, item names, descriptions and sections. The layout itself is the same clean design for every ArtOfMenu menu. There are no themes to choose from and no custom HTML or CSS.

faq.q: What makes a good QR code menu design?
faq.a: Readable text at phone size, photos for the dishes that need them, one-line descriptions, allergens on each item and sections that match how guests order. A shorter list of strong items usually looks better than a long one.

faq.q: Do I need a designer to make a beautiful digital menu?
faq.a: Not with ArtOfMenu. The layout is already designed. What makes the difference is the quality of your photos and how clearly you describe each item. An afternoon with a phone camera before service is a good place to start.

faq.q: How should the printed QR code look on the table?
faq.a: Keep the code large and high-contrast so it scans in low light, add a short line such as “Scan for the menu” and put your colors around the code rather than on it. Test it with a few phones before printing a batch.

faq.q: Does the menu show my business name?
faq.a: Yes. It opens on your own domain, so your name is in the address bar from the moment the menu loads. Guests who hesitate before tapping an unfamiliar link can see at a glance that the menu is yours.

body: When the temperature drops, hot drinks move up the menu. Cold drinks and items about to run out move down. A guest scanning on a cold morning sees the hot chocolate first, and a guest ordering late in the day is not steered toward a dish with two portions left.
During the day, only the order changes. Prices stay fixed until the next day.

When a guest adds an item, the menu shows the item most often ordered with it at that branch. It learns from your own orders, so it suggests what your guests actually pair: fries with the burger, or the cheesecake your regulars take with an espresso.

It also learns from anonymized behavior coefficients of similar businesses. It never uses their prices, and your prices are never shared with anyone.
bullets: Approve: you see tomorrow's prices and confirm each one
Automatic: prices update inside your limits without a step from you
Off: the menu uses your base prices

body: Guests notice when a coffee costs far more than it did yesterday. That is why every price stays between a minimum and maximum you choose, and why nothing changes during service. sections.h2: QR menu maker or QR code generator?
body: A QR code generator only makes the code: a square that points to a link. If that link is a PDF file, guests get a document they have to pinch and zoom, and every change means uploading a new file.
A QR menu maker builds the menu itself, with items, photos, allergens and languages, and you edit it online behind a code that stays the same. ArtOfMenu works this way, starting from your PDF.

Test the code before you print a batch. Scan it with two or three different phones, in the lighting of your own dining room at night. Avoid glossy laminate that reflects ceiling lights, and on outdoor tables use weatherproof stickers or stands that will not blow over.

When a price changes, edit it in the menu, and the next scan shows it. When a dish comes off the menu, remove it. On the Smart plan, recipe-based stock marks items sold out on their own when an ingredient runs out, so you do not have to remember mid-service.

faq.q: How do I create a QR code for my menu?

faq.q: Can I just link a QR code to my PDF menu?

faq.q: What size should a QR code be on a table?

faq.q: Do I need to reprint the QR code when the menu changes?

restaurant-sales.title: How to Increase Restaurant Sales | ArtOfMenu Guide
restaurant-sales.description: Practical ways to increase restaurant sales without more advertising: menu layout, pricing, average check, table turns, waste and staff.
restaurant-sales.h1: How to increase restaurant sales with what you already have.
restaurant-sales.lead: The most reliable ways to increase restaurant sales come from inside the restaurant: a clearer menu, deliberate prices, a higher average check, faster table turns and less waste. Marketing brings guests in, and these levers decide what each visit is worth.
restaurant-sales.answer: To increase restaurant sales, work on five levers: how many guests you serve, how often tables turn at peak, how much each guest spends, how much food you waste and how well your staff sell. Much of the gain comes from menu layout, pricing and service speed rather than advertising. ArtOfMenu's menu reports and table ordering help with some of these, but the method works on paper too.

body: Sales are covers multiplied by average check. Before changing anything, write down three figures for a normal week: covers per service, average spend per guest and how many tables you turn more than once at peak. Do this separately for lunch and dinner, and for weekdays and weekends, because they often behave like different businesses.
Then change one lever at a time and give it two or three weeks. If you change the menu, the prices and the staff rota in the same month, you will not know which change worked.

Guests read menus quickly. They notice the first items in each section, anything with a photo and anything set apart from the list. Put your most profitable dishes in those spots, and keep the cheapest filler items out of them.
Cut what does not sell. A long list of mains takes longer to read and longer to cook, and it ties up more stock. A shorter menu of dishes that sell or earn well makes each choice easier.

On a digital menu you can test this. Move a dish to the top of its section for two weeks and compare the orders. ArtOfMenu's menu reports flag items guests see but rarely open, and items they open but never order, which tells you whether the problem is visibility or the dish itself.

Look at the contribution margin of each dish: the price minus the cost of its ingredients. A $24 pasta with $5 of ingredients earns $19 a plate, more than a $32 steak with $15 of ingredients. That is why the cheaper dish may deserve the better spot on the menu.

Raise prices first on dishes guests love and cannot easily compare elsewhere, such as your house specialties. Be careful with items that have an obvious market price, like a well-known bottled beer. Make small changes, a few dishes at a time, and watch orders for several weeks.
If your demand swings with the weather or special days, ArtOfMenu's Smart plan can set tomorrow's prices each evening inside a minimum and maximum you choose. Prices never change during service.
Upselling works when it is specific. “Would you like anything else?” invites a no. “The burrata goes well with that tomato salad” gives the guest something concrete to say yes to.
bullets: Choose one add-on for each main: a side, a sauce or a glass of wine that suits it
Make starters and sharing plates easy to add for groups
Offer dessert and coffee at the right moment, as the main plates are cleared
Offer a premium version of a top seller, such as a larger cut or an extra topping

sections.h2: Turn tables faster at peak without rushing guests
body: At peak, the slow moments are rarely the meal itself. They are waiting to order, waiting for the check and waiting for the table to be reset. Time each step on a busy night and the gaps usually become obvious.

Let guests read the menu before they sit. Take drink orders straight away. Bring the check when the dessert plates go. With table ordering, guests send orders when they are ready instead of waiting to catch a server, and on ArtOfMenu's Smart plan they can also ask for the bill from the table.
Keep peak tactics for peak hours. At 3 pm, a guest who stays for another coffee is adding to the check.

sections.h2: Cut waste and protect the margin
body: Every portion you throw away is food you paid for and never sold. Track waste for two weeks: what was thrown away, why and what it cost. Over-prepping, over-ordering and dishes nobody orders are the usual causes.

Standardize portions with recipe cards and scales, count stock regularly and drop dishes whose ingredients you buy for that dish alone. Our restaurant inventory guide walks through the method step by step.

Your team shapes much of the average check. Let every server taste the menu, give them two dishes to recommend each shift and explain why those dishes matter. A ten-minute briefing before service on what is fresh, what is running low and what to suggest sets the tone for the whole night. Recognize the people who sell well, and pair new staff with them.

A returning guest needs no ad to find you. Remember regulars by name, collect email addresses from guests who agree to it and tell them when the seasonal menu changes. Reply to reviews politely and fix what they point to. Steady repeat visits do more for weekly sales than a one-off promotion.

faq.q: How can I increase restaurant sales without advertising?
faq.a: Work on what each visit is worth. Clean up the menu layout, raise prices on dishes guests love, suggest specific add-ons, speed up ordering and payment at peak and cut waste. None of this needs an ad budget, and it affects every guest you already serve.

faq.q: What is the quickest way to raise the average check?
faq.a: Specific suggestions. Pair each main with one side or drink and have staff recommend it by name. On a digital menu, show a pairing when a guest adds an item. Dessert and coffee prompts as plates are cleared also help.

faq.q: Should I raise my menu prices?
faq.a: Raise them selectively. Start with popular dishes that guests do not easily compare elsewhere, change a few at a time and watch orders for several weeks. Avoid big jumps on items with obvious market prices, such as well-known bottled drinks.

faq.q: How do I know which dishes to remove?
faq.a: Compare each dish's popularity with its contribution margin. Dishes that sell little and earn little are the first candidates. Our menu engineering guide explains the full method, including the stars, plowhorses, puzzles and dogs matrix.

faq.q: Does a QR menu increase restaurant sales?
faq.a: A QR menu on its own guarantees nothing. It helps when you use it well: putting profitable dishes where guests look, showing photos, suggesting pairings and letting guests order without waiting. ArtOfMenu adds reports that show which items guests ignore.

bar-sales.description: Ways to increase bar and pub sales: a sharper drinks menu, a happy hour that pays, faster rounds, premium spirits, food pairing and tighter stock.
bar-sales.h1: How to increase bar sales, one round at a time.
bar-sales.lead: To increase bar sales, speed up service, build a drinks menu that steers guests toward better-margin drinks and control stock so pour costs stay honest. Each of these can be measured on a normal Friday night.
bar-sales.answer: Bar sales grow when guests order more rounds, trade up to better drinks and stay a little longer, while pour costs stay under control. The main levers are a focused drinks menu, faster service, a happy hour that fills quiet hours, premium suggestions, food that suits drinks and accurate stock. ArtOfMenu's table ordering and recipe-based stock help with speed and sold-out drinks.

sections.h2: Measure the night before changing it
body: Track three figures for each type of night: guests, average spend per guest and pour cost. Pour cost is the cost of what you poured divided by drink sales, and it tells you whether a busy night actually made money.
Work it out by category. Draft beer, wine, cocktails and spirits each have their own normal range, and the gap between what your count says you used and what you sold is where money leaks.

sections.h2: Build a drinks menu that sells
body: Listing every spirit you stock makes for a long read and a slow decision. Guests choose faster when the menu has a clear structure: signature cocktails, classics, beer by style, wine by the glass and a short spirits section.

Put your signatures first and give each one a line of ingredients. Signatures are where you set the price, because nobody can compare them with the bar next door. Keep the list short enough that every drink can be made well at speed, and review it each season. Retire drinks that sell slowly and need ingredients nothing else uses.
On a busy night, sales are limited by how fast you take orders and pour. Every minute a group waits to order is a minute without the next round.
bullets: Batch the prep for your top cocktails before service
Set up stations so the most-ordered bottles are within reach
Let table guests order without having to wave for attention
Clear empty glasses quickly and ask about the next round as you do

sections.h2: Run a happy hour that pays
body: Happy hour should fill hours that would otherwise be quiet. If 6 pm is already busy, a discount there only gives margin away. Choose drinks that still earn a healthy margin at the lower price, keep the offer simple and end it before your natural peak.
Pair it with food. A plate of something salty gives a table a reason to stay for a second drink. Check the rules where you operate first, since some areas restrict drink promotions.

When a guest orders a gin and tonic, a server who asks “our house gin, or the one from the local distillery?” turns a basic drink into a premium one with a single question. Train staff on two or three premium options per category and let them taste each one, so the suggestion sounds like advice rather than a script.

sections.h2: Sell food that keeps people at the table
body: Salty, shareable food keeps a table ordering: fries, nuts, flatbreads, sliders. It also slows the drinking down, which keeps the evening pleasant for everyone in the room. Put two or three bar snacks right next to the drinks rather than on a separate page.
On ArtOfMenu's Smart plan, when a guest adds a drink, the menu suggests the item most often ordered with it at your bar.
Count spirits weekly, by bottle and estimated fraction, and compare usage with sales. Use jiggers or measured pourers for every drink, including the ones your bartender has made a thousand times.

Watch the drinks that depend on fresh ingredients. When limes or mint run out mid-service, guests keep ordering what you cannot make. With recipe-based stock on ArtOfMenu's Smart plan, one ingredient running out marks every drink made with it as sold out on its own. On the Order plan, simple stock and order reports show what each night used.

sections.h2: Give people a reason to come on a Tuesday
body: Quiet nights need their own plan: a quiz, a local band, a tasting night with a nearby brewery or a weekly food special. Pick one, run it on the same night every week for long enough to build a habit and tell your regulars about it in person.

faq.q: How do I increase beer sales in a bar?
faq.a: Keep draft lines clean and beer fresh, describe each beer by style on the menu, offer a tasting flight for undecided guests and rotate one guest tap so regulars have something new. Pair beers with salty snacks and offer a second pint when you clear the first glass.

faq.q: How can I increase liquor sales in a restaurant?
faq.a: Suggest a drink with every food order, by name. Train servers on a few wine and cocktail pairings, show drinks next to dishes on the menu and offer a premium spirit when a guest orders a mixed drink.

faq.q: Does happy hour actually increase bar sales?
faq.a: It can, if it fills quiet hours and the discounted drinks still earn a margin. It loses money when it discounts hours that would be busy anyway. Check local rules too, since some areas restrict drink promotions.

faq.q: How can I serve drinks faster on busy nights?
faq.a: Batch cocktail prep before service, set up stations around your top sellers, keep glassware stocked and let table guests order from their phones. On ArtOfMenu's Order plan, those orders reach staff phones instantly.

faq.q: How often should I count bar inventory?
faq.a: Weekly for spirits and wine, plus a full count at the end of every month. Compare what you used with what you sold. Large gaps point to over-pouring, unrecorded comps or breakage.

cafe-sales.description: How to increase café revenue: a faster morning rush, add-ons, food pairing, weather-ready menus, loyalty and less waste. Practical steps for owners.
cafe-sales.h1: How to increase cafe sales from the first coffee of the day.
cafe-sales.lead: To increase café sales, serve the morning rush faster, sell one more item with each coffee and match the menu to the weather and the season. Small changes to the average ticket add up quickly when most tickets are a single drink.

The practical levers are a faster morning rush, add-ons like extra shots and milk options, food paired with drinks, a menu that follows weather and season, loyalty for regulars and less pastry and milk waste. body: In many cafés, a few short windows carry much of the day's takings. Pull your sales in 15-minute blocks for a few weeks and see whether that is true for you. Those windows decide your staffing, your prep and which drinks belong at the top of the menu.
Compare weekdays with weekends as well. A café near offices and a café near a park can have opposite weeks.
In the morning, speed is revenue. A person who sees a queue out the door often walks on to the next café.
bullets: Put the menu where people can read it while they queue, including a QR code by the line
Keep the most-ordered drinks at the top and the board short
Bake and bag the top pastries before opening

body: A coffee-only ticket is small. A pastry, a second shot or a larger size changes the day's total. Train baristas to suggest one specific item. “Our banana bread is still warm” gives a guest something to say yes to in a way “Anything else?” does not.
ArtOfMenu's Smart plan does this on the menu itself: when a guest adds a drink, it shows the item most often ordered with it at your branch.
bullets: Price sizes so the larger one feels like the better deal
Charge clearly for extras such as oat milk, syrups and extra shots
Offer a morning drink-and-pastry pairing at a modest saving
Put food next to the drinks it suits instead of on a separate list

sections.h2: Let the weather set the menu
body: Cafés feel the weather quickly. A cold, wet morning sells hot chocolate, soup and porridge, and a heatwave sells iced drinks. Check the forecast the night before and adjust prep: fewer iced items before a rainy Tuesday, more milk and pastries before a cold weekend.

On a digital menu, the order can change too. ArtOfMenu's weather-aware order moves hot drinks up when it gets cold, and moves cold drinks and items about to run out down. Prices stay the same throughout the day.

sections.h2: Plan seasonal drinks like small launches
body: Seasonal drinks give regulars a reason to try something new, and they carry a price that nobody compares with a standard latte. Plan each one: cost the recipe, set the price, train the team, photograph the drink and decide in advance when it ends. A clear end date gives guests a reason to try it this week.

sections.h2: Reward regulars without giving margin away
body: Regulars are the base of a café's income. A stamp card works, and so does remembering a name and an order. If you run a loyalty card, make the reward a visit at a quieter hour or a food item, rather than another drink at the morning peak when you are already full.

Unsold pastries at closing and milk poured down the drain are two familiar café losses. Track what you throw away each day for two weeks. Bake to your real sales by weekday instead of a fixed number, offer a late-day bundle and use milk pitchers sized to the drink.
Recipe-based stock on ArtOfMenu's Smart plan marks drinks as sold out when an ingredient such as oat milk runs out, so guests do not order something you cannot make.

Afternoons are often quiet. Think about what your neighborhood wants after 2 pm: a calm place to work, cake and a pot of tea for two, or an early-evening drink if your license allows it. Give that one clear line on the menu and one sign in the window.

faq.q: How can I increase sales in my cafe?
faq.a: Serve the peak faster, suggest one specific item with every drink, match the menu and prep to the weather, plan seasonal drinks with clear end dates and reward regulars at quieter hours. Track waste so the extra sales are not lost to unsold pastries.

faq.q: How do I increase cafe profit, not just revenue?
faq.a: Check the margin of every item, since some drinks and foods earn far more than others. Price extras clearly, drop slow items, bake to real demand and check portion sizes, so more of each sale stays with you.

faq.q: Can a small cafe be profitable?
faq.a: Yes, when rent, staffing and waste fit the volume you can realistically serve. Small cafés that do well tend to know their peak hours, keep a focused menu, control waste and get regulars to add food to their coffee.

faq.q: Do seasonal drinks increase cafe revenue?
faq.a: They can. A seasonal drink gives regulars something new and carries a price that is not compared with a standard latte. Cost it properly, promote it from the first day and set an end date.

faq.q: What should I put next to coffee on the menu?
faq.a: Items guests naturally pair: a croissant or banana bread with a latte, a cookie with a cold brew, a sandwich at lunch. Place them beside the drinks, and on a digital menu show the pairing when a guest adds a coffee.

menu-engineering.title: Menu Engineering: Matrix, Formula and Steps | ArtOfMenu
menu-engineering.description: Menu engineering explained: contribution margin, popularity, the stars, plowhorses, puzzles and dogs matrix, plus a worked step-by-step method.
menu-engineering.h1: Menu engineering, explained step by step.
menu-engineering.lead: Menu engineering is a method for deciding what to keep, reprice, reposition or remove on your menu by comparing each item's popularity with its contribution margin. You can do it with a spreadsheet and last month's sales.
menu-engineering.answer: Menu engineering analyzes each menu item on two measures: how popular it is and how much it earns per sale after food cost, known as contribution margin. Items fall into four groups, stars, plowhorses, puzzles and dogs, from the matrix Michael Kasavana and Donald Smith published in 1982. Each group calls for a different action. ArtOfMenu's menu reports add what guests look at but skip.

body: Contribution margin is the selling price minus the food cost of one portion. If a risotto sells for $22 and its ingredients cost $6, its contribution margin is $16. Use the price before sales tax or VAT.
Popularity is the item's share of sales within its category. Compare mains with mains and desserts with desserts, never across categories, because a guest who orders a main is choosing among mains.

In the original method, an item counts as popular if its share of sales in its category is at least 70% of an equal share. With 10 mains, an equal share is 10%, so a main is popular if it accounts for 7% or more of main-course sales. The 70% line stops items from being labeled unpopular just for being slightly below average.
For margin, compare each item's contribution margin with the weighted average for its category: the total contribution margin of the category divided by the total number of items sold in it.

sections.h2: The menu engineering matrix: four quadrants
body: The labels sound blunt, but they make menu meetings faster, because each one comes with a clear default action.
bullets: Stars: high popularity, high margin. Keep them visible, keep quality consistent and test small price rises.
Plowhorses: high popularity, low margin. Raise the price a little, trim the portion cost or pair them with a high-margin side.
Puzzles: low popularity, high margin. Move them to better spots, rename them, add a photo or have staff recommend them.
Dogs: low popularity, low margin. Remove them, unless they serve a clear purpose, such as a children's dish or the vegetarian option a group needs.

body: Say your dessert section sold 400 portions last month across five desserts. An equal share is 20%, so the popularity line is 14%, or 56 portions. The tiramisu sold 120 at a $7 margin. The lemon tart sold 40 at a $9 margin. The weighted average margin across all five desserts comes to $6.50.

The tiramisu is a star: popular and above the average margin. The lemon tart is a puzzle: it earns well but sits below the popularity line, so it needs better placement, a photo or a server's recommendation before you consider removing it.

The spreadsheet tells you what to change, and the layout is where much of the change happens. Puzzles in particular are often a visibility problem. Guests tend to notice the first and last items in a section, items with a photo and items set apart with a box or extra space.

Describe dishes in concrete terms, and avoid lining prices up in a neat column, which invites guests to scan for the cheapest. On a QR menu, the top of each section is the spot to give your stars and puzzles.

Classic menu engineering only sees what was sold. A digital menu can also show what guests looked at. ArtOfMenu's menu reports flag two patterns: items that are seen but rarely opened, and items that are opened but never ordered.

The first usually points to a name, photo or position problem. The second points to what guests see after opening the item: the price, the description or the portion in the photo. For a puzzle, that tells you which fix to try first.
Repricing is one of the main actions the matrix suggests, especially for plowhorses. Make changes in small steps and watch whether popularity holds.

ArtOfMenu's Smart plan adds daily pricing: each evening it sets tomorrow's prices from the branch location, weather, special days and expected demand, inside the minimum and maximum you set per item. Menu engineering helps you choose those limits. A star can often carry a wider range, while a plowhorse that guests compare with other places may need a narrow one.
Most menu engineering errors come from the data that goes into the matrix.
bullets: Using last year's recipe costs after supplier prices have moved
Comparing items across categories
Analyzing a period with a holiday or closure that distorts sales
Changing price, position and description at once, so you cannot tell what worked
Removing a dog that a regular group orders every week without asking why

steps.h2: How to do menu engineering in seven steps

items.d: Use four to eight normal weeks of sales. Leave out holidays and closures, or analyze them separately.
Work out the food cost of one portion of each item, including garnishes and included sides, at current supplier prices.
Pull the number sold for each item from your POS, grouped by category.
For each item, subtract the portion cost from the price before tax, then multiply by items sold for its total contribution.
Popularity: 70% of an equal share in the category. Margin: total category contribution divided by total items sold.
Mark each item as a star, plowhorse, puzzle or dog, and choose one action for each.
Make the changes, leave them for at least a month and repeat the analysis with the new sales.

faq.q: What is menu engineering?
faq.a: It is a way of analyzing a menu by each item's popularity and contribution margin, then deciding what to promote, reprice, reposition or remove. Michael Kasavana and Donald Smith set it out in 1982, and it is still widely taught in hospitality courses.

faq.q: What is the menu engineering formula?
faq.a: Contribution margin equals selling price minus food cost per portion. An item is popular if its sales share in its category is at least 70% of an equal share. It is high-margin if its contribution margin is above the category's weighted average.

faq.q: What are stars, plowhorses, puzzles and dogs?
faq.a: Stars are popular and profitable. Plowhorses are popular but earn little. Puzzles earn well but sell little. Dogs sell little and earn little. Each needs a different action: protect, reprice, reposition or remove.

faq.q: How often should I do menu engineering?
faq.a: Every quarter is a practical rhythm, plus after any major supplier price change or menu update. If you run seasonal menus, analyze each one at the end of its season.

faq.q: Can I do a menu engineering worksheet in Excel?
faq.a: Yes. A spreadsheet with item, category, items sold, price, portion cost and contribution margin is enough. Add two formulas for the thresholds and one column for the quadrant, then refresh it each quarter with new sales and costs.

inventory.title: Restaurant Inventory Management: Step by Step | ArtOfMenu
inventory.description: A practical guide to restaurant inventory: counting, recipe costing, par levels, FIFO and waste tracking, plus recipe stock that marks items sold out.
inventory.lead: Restaurant inventory management means knowing what you have, what you should have used and what you actually used, then closing the gap between the last two. It rests on regular counts, costed recipes, par levels and first-in, first-out storage.
inventory.answer: Restaurant inventory management is the routine of counting stock, costing recipes, setting par levels and rotating stock first in, first out, so food cost matches sales. The core check compares what your recipes say you used with what the count shows. ArtOfMenu's Order plan includes simple stock reports, and its Smart plan uses recipe-based stock to mark items sold out when an ingredient runs out.

sections.h2: Why inventory decides your food cost
body: Food cost percentage is the cost of food used divided by food sales. The cost of food used is opening stock plus purchases minus closing stock. Without an accurate count at both ends, that number is a guess, and every pricing decision built on it carries the same error.

A count is only quick if the storeroom is arranged for it. Lay out the count sheet in the same order as the shelves, from the walk-in to dry storage to the bar. Use one unit per item and stick to it: count olive oil by the bottle every time, never by the case one week and the bottle the next.

Count high-value and fast-moving items, such as proteins, dairy and spirits, every week. Count everything once a month. Have the same two people count, on the same day and at the same time, before deliveries arrive.

A recipe card lists every ingredient in a dish with its quantity and cost. Use the usable yield, not the purchase weight. A case of whole fish or a bunch of herbs loses weight in trimming, so the real cost per ounce is higher than the invoice suggests.
Recheck the cards whenever an invoice price moves noticeably. A recipe card is only useful while its prices are current.
A par level is the amount of an item you want on hand to last until the next delivery, plus a safety buffer. A simple formula: average daily usage × days between deliveries + safety stock.

If you use 12 lb of chicken thighs a day, get deliveries every 3 days and want one day of buffer, your par is 12 × 3 + 12 = 48 lb. When you order, order up to par: with 18 lb on the shelf, order 30. Review pars monthly and before the season turns, because opening the terrace in May changes your usage.

FIFO means the oldest stock is used first. Put new deliveries behind existing stock, label every container with the date it arrived or was prepped and check dates on every shift. It reduces spoilage and keeps food safe, and it makes the walk-in easier to count.
Keep a waste sheet in the kitchen with the item, quantity, reason (spoiled, over-prepped, dropped, sent back) and who logged it. Two weeks of honest entries show patterns nobody notices day to day.

Then compare theoretical usage with actual usage. Theoretical usage is items sold multiplied by recipe quantities. Actual usage is opening stock plus purchases minus closing stock. The difference, called variance, comes from portioning, waste, theft or counting errors. Investigate the largest variances by value first.

sections.h2: Keep the menu in step with stock
body: A guest who orders a dish and hears ten minutes later that it is gone has a worse evening, and the server has an awkward conversation. When an ingredient runs out, every dish that uses it should come off the menu at once.

ArtOfMenu's Smart plan does this with recipe-based stock: link each item to its ingredients, and when one runs out, every item made with it shows as sold out on its own. Its weather-aware order also moves items that are about to run out further down the menu. On the Order plan, simple stock and order reports help you see what moved and plan purchases.

A spreadsheet works for one location with a stable menu: one tab for the count, one for recipe costs and one for par levels. Software starts to earn its cost when you run several branches, change the menu often or want the team to count on a phone. Either way, the weekly routine is what keeps the numbers right.

steps.h2: Set up inventory control in seven steps

items.d: Write down everything you buy, grouped by storage area, with one counting unit for each.
Count everything before service on a fixed day and record the value at current invoice prices.
Build a recipe card for each dish with quantities, yields and ingredient costs.
Use daily usage × days between deliveries + safety stock, and always order up to par.
Date every delivery and prep container, and store new stock behind old.
Record what is thrown away and why, on a sheet kept where the waste happens.
Each week, compare theoretical with actual usage and act on the largest gaps first.

faq.q: What is restaurant inventory management?
faq.a: It is the process of tracking the food and drink you buy, store and use, so you order the right amounts, waste less and know your real food cost. It covers counting, recipe costing, par levels, stock rotation and waste tracking.

faq.q: How often should a restaurant do inventory?
faq.a: Count high-value and fast-moving items, such as proteins, dairy and spirits, weekly. Do a full count of everything at least monthly, on the same day and at the same time, before deliveries arrive.

faq.q: How do I calculate par levels?
faq.a: Multiply average daily usage by the number of days between deliveries, then add safety stock. When ordering, order the difference between your par level and what you have on hand.

faq.q: What is the FIFO method in a restaurant?
faq.a: First in, first out: older stock is used before newer stock. Store new deliveries behind existing ones and label everything with a date. It reduces spoilage and keeps food safe.

faq.q: Can I manage restaurant inventory in Excel?
faq.a: Yes, for a single location with a stable menu. Use one sheet for counts, one for recipe costs and one for par levels. Software becomes more useful with several branches or a menu that changes often.

faq.q: Can stock levels update my menu automatically?
faq.a: With ArtOfMenu's Smart plan, yes. Recipe-based stock links each item to its ingredients. When an ingredient runs out, every item made with it shows as sold out on the menu on its own.
